body:
Why electricity needs to be stored

Electricity generation and electricity consumption must remain balanced for a power system to operate reliably. However, electricity demand changes throughout the day, and some sources of electricity do not generate continuously.

Solar photovoltaic panels generate electricity when sufficient sunlight is available. Their output falls in the evening, when electricity demand may still be high. Wind generation also varies with wind conditions. An energy storage system can absorb electricity when it is available and release useful energy later.

For example, a solar power plant may generate more electricity than the grid needs at midday. Instead of reducing all the surplus generation, part of that electricity can charge a battery or pump water to a higher reservoir. The stored energy can then support electricity supply during the evening.

Energy storage is the process of converting energy into a form that can be retained and subsequently recovered for use. Electricity storage systems commonly store energy in chemical, gravitational, mechanical or thermal forms.

Storage does not create additional energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change form. A battery stores energy through reversible electrochemical changes. A pumped-storage plant uses electricity to raise water and store gravitational potential energy.

During charging or pumping, the system takes energy from an external source. During discharge, it returns part of that energy as electricity. Some energy is lost as heat, friction or other less useful forms during conversion.

Therefore, a storage plant is not automatically a primary source of energy. It normally shifts the availability of energy from one time to another. The environmental benefit depends partly on the electricity used to charge it and the generation it subsequently replaces.

Power and energy are different quantities

Power measures how rapidly energy is transferred. Energy measures the total amount transferred over a period.

QuantityCommon unitMeaning for storage
Power ratingkW, MW or GWHow rapidly a system can charge or discharge
Energy capacitykWh, MWh or GWhHow much energy a system can store or deliver under stated conditions
Discharge durationHoursHow long the system can supply a specified power
Round-trip efficiencyPercentageHow much delivered energy is recovered relative to the energy supplied for storage

A storage system rated at 100 MW and 400 MWh has a nominal discharge duration of 4 hours at 100 MW, assuming its full stated energy capacity is available at that output:

Duration = 400 MWh ÷ 100 MW = 4 hours.

In practice, available duration also depends on the usable energy window, operating limits, temperature, ageing and the point at which power is measured.

Round-trip efficiency and stored-energy losses

Round-trip efficiency is the ratio of useful energy recovered after storage to the energy supplied to the storage system over the complete cycle, measured at consistently defined boundaries.

Suppose an illustrative system receives 100 MWh of electricity during charging and later delivers 80 MWh. Its electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is 80%. The remaining 20 MWh is not destroyed; it is converted into less useful forms or consumed by associated equipment.

Round-trip efficiency must not be confused with discharge efficiency alone. Pumping losses, battery charging losses and the electricity consumed by cooling or other auxiliary systems may all affect the complete result.

State of charge and available energy

The state of charge indicates the remaining charge in a battery relative to its defined capacity. A battery at 50% state of charge is not necessarily capable of delivering half its original, new-battery energy rating. Its present usable capacity may have fallen through ageing, and some energy may be reserved for protection or reliability.

Storage technologies also differ in the duration for which they are useful. Some respond quickly and supply electricity for seconds or minutes; others are designed for several hours or potentially much longer periods. These ranges are typical applications, not absolute boundaries.

Prelims focus

  • MW measures power; MWh measures energy.
  • A 100 MW, 400 MWh system has a nominal full-power duration of 4 hours.
  • Round-trip efficiency compares useful energy recovered with energy supplied for storage.
  • Energy storage shifts energy between times; it does not create energy.
  • Trap: A storage plant rated at 100 MW does not necessarily contain 100 MWh of usable energy.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Work and Energy, printed pp. 153–156; Ministry of Power, Government of India, National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems, August 2023, Sections 1 and 4, pp. 1–3; U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Integration: Solar Energy and Storage Basics, sections on energy storage, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Electricity Storage: Purpose, Power, Energy and Duration

body:
How a rechargeable battery works

A battery contains one or more electrochemical cells. Each cell converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy through oxidation and reduction reactions. In a rechargeable battery, an external supply can drive the reactions in the reverse direction and restore much of the cell's stored energy.

A cell that can be recharged is called a secondary cell. A non-rechargeable cell intended for discharge without subsequent recharging is called a primary cell. Lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles, phones and grid storage are secondary batteries.

In a lithium-ion cell, lithium ions move between 2 electrode materials. Most conventional lithium-ion cells use a carbon-based material, commonly graphite, at the negative electrode. The positive electrode contains a lithium-bearing compound such as lithium iron phosphate or a lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide.

The principal cell components

ComponentFunction
Negative electrodeCommonly graphite; hosts lithium during the charged state
Positive electrodeA lithium-containing compound that receives lithium ions during discharge
ElectrolyteAllows ions to move between the electrodes
SeparatorPrevents direct electrical contact between electrodes while permitting ionic movement through the electrolyte
Current collectorsConduct electrons between the electrode materials and the external circuit
Cell enclosureContains and protects the electrochemical assembly

Conventional lithium-ion electrolytes commonly contain a lithium salt in an organic liquid. The electrolyte conducts ions, whereas electrons move through the external electrical circuit during useful discharge. The separator helps prevent a direct internal short circuit.

What happens during discharge?

When a charged lithium-ion cell supplies electricity to a device, lithium ions move through the electrolyte from the negative graphite electrode towards the positive electrode. At the same time, electrons travel from the negative terminal through the external circuit to the positive terminal.

The moving electrons can power a lamp, motor or other electrical load. The movement of lithium ions inside the cell maintains the electrochemical balance needed for the reaction to continue.

In common battery terminology, the anode is the negative electrode during discharge, where oxidation occurs, and the cathode is the positive electrode during discharge, where reduction occurs.

What happens during charging?

Charging reverses the overall process. An external electrical supply drives lithium ions from the positive electrode back towards the negative graphite electrode. Electrons are also driven through the external electrical connections in the corresponding reverse direction.

The charged cell can later release energy again. This repeated movement of lithium ions between host materials is the central working principle of the lithium-ion battery.

The names anode and cathode are commonly retained for the negative and positive electrodes of a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, even while charging reverses the reactions. In strict electrochemical terminology, oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode; their reaction roles therefore reverse during charging.

Why lithium-ion batteries are widely used

Lithium-ion batteries generally offer relatively high energy density, good electrical efficiency and repeated rechargeability. Energy density means the amount of stored energy relative to mass or volume. High energy density is particularly valuable in mobile phones and electric vehicles, where weight and space matter.

For stationary electricity storage, the choice of battery also depends on safety, service life, cost, available space and the expected number of cycles. The lightest battery is not necessarily the best battery for a fixed grid installation.

Conventional lithium-ion cells use lithium ions held within electrode materials. They should not be confused with rechargeable lithium-metal designs, which use metallic lithium at the negative electrode and have different technical characteristics.

Prelims focus

  • Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable secondary batteries.
  • Graphite is a common negative-electrode material.
  • During discharge, lithium ions move towards the positive electrode.
  • Electrons supply the external load; ions move through the electrolyte.
  • The separator prevents direct contact between the electrodes.
  • Trap: Lithium ions and electrons do not travel along the same path through the cell.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Lithium-ion Batteries: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, Background and Chemistries and Components, printed pp. 1–2; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, printed pp. 175–178; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, printed pp. 116–119; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Lithium-Ion Batteries: Cell Components and Working Principle

body:
Not all rechargeable batteries use the same chemistry

Rechargeable batteries operate through reversible electrochemical reactions, but the materials participating in these reactions differ. Those material differences influence energy density, safety, weight, charging behaviour, service life and suitability for particular applications.

Even within lithium-ion batteries, several chemistries exist. The names commonly used for lithium-ion variants refer mainly to their positive-electrode materials.

Lithium iron phosphate and nickel manganese cobalt

Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) uses a lithium iron phosphate positive electrode. It does not require nickel or cobalt in that positive-electrode material. LFP is valued for its thermal stability, useful cycle life and suitability for stationary electricity storage. Its energy density is generally lower than that of high-energy nickel-rich lithium-ion variants.

Lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) uses a positive-electrode material containing nickel, manganese and cobalt. NMC variants are used where a combination of energy density and battery performance is important, including many electric-vehicle applications.

Both LFP and NMC are lithium-ion batteries. Neither should be described as a non-lithium alternative. Their relative safety, price and lifetime depend on their specific formulation and system design; no chemistry is automatically superior in every application.

LFP: Lithium, iron and phosphate in the positive-electrode material; no nickel or cobalt is required there. NMC: Lithium with nickel, manganese and cobalt in the positive-electrode material. Both involve movement of lithium ions.

Alternatives to conventional lithium-ion cells

Battery typeBasic principleUseful distinction
LFP lithium-ionLithium ions move between electrodes; iron-phosphate positive electrodeGood thermal stability and cycle-life characteristics
NMC lithium-ionLithium ions move between electrodes; nickel-manganese-cobalt positive electrodeCommonly offers higher energy density than LFP
Lead-acidReversible reactions involving lead-based electrodes and sulfuric acidEstablished, relatively heavy technology; lead requires careful recycling
Sodium-ionSodium ions move between suitable electrode materialsDoes not depend on lithium as the charge-carrying ion
Redox flow batteryElectroactive materials in liquid electrolytes circulate through a cell stackEnergy capacity can be increased by enlarging electrolyte storage

Lead-acid batteries

Lead-acid batteries are an older rechargeable technology. They commonly use lead and lead-dioxide electrodes with a sulfuric-acid electrolyte. Their established applications include vehicle starting, backup power and certain stationary installations. They are heavier and generally have lower energy density than lithium-ion batteries.

Because lead is toxic, collection and proper recycling are especially important. The continuing use of lead-acid batteries demonstrates that a newer battery chemistry does not eliminate every established application of an older one.

Sodium-ion batteries

Sodium-ion batteries use sodium ions rather than lithium ions as the principal charge carriers. Sodium is widely available, and these batteries can reduce dependence on lithium-based materials. However, their actual cost and performance depend on electrode chemistry, manufacturing scale and other factors. They should not be assumed to have higher energy density than lithium-ion batteries.

Redox flow batteries

In a redox flow battery, electroactive substances are stored in external electrolyte tanks. Pumps circulate these liquids through an electrochemical cell stack, where charging and discharging reactions take place.

The cell stack largely determines the system's power capability, while the amount of electrolyte helps determine its energy capacity. This distinction makes flow batteries interesting for stationary storage lasting several hours or longer. They require tanks, pumps and associated equipment, so their construction differs from that of sealed lithium-ion cells.

Vanadium redox flow batteries are an important example. The word flow refers to the circulation of electrolyte; it does not mean that electricity itself flows through the tanks.

Developing technologies

Solid-state batteries replace some or all of the conventional liquid-electrolyte arrangement with solid ion-conducting materials. They are being developed to improve selected performance and safety characteristics, but their properties depend on the exact design. The term solid-state alone does not establish that a cell is non-flammable, inexpensive or commercially mature.

Other electrochemical storage families include nickel-based batteries and high-temperature sodium batteries. Their suitability depends on application requirements rather than a universal ranking of battery types.

Prelims focus

  • LFP and NMC are both lithium-ion chemistries.
  • LFP positive-electrode material does not require nickel or cobalt.
  • Sodium-ion batteries use sodium ions instead of lithium ions.
  • Lead-acid batteries contain lead-based electrodes and sulfuric-acid electrolyte.
  • Flow batteries store electroactive liquids in external tanks.
  • Trap: LFP is not a lithium-free battery.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Lithium-ion Batteries: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, Chemistries and Components, printed p. 1; International Energy Agency, Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions, Executive Summary, 25 April 2024, sections on lithium-ion chemistry and alternatives; U.S. Department of Energy, Battery Energy Storage Systems: Considerations for Implementation, 5 August 2025, slide 12; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
